exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \begin{align*} u=y^2+4 \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y} = 2y, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} = e^{2y+1} \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\, \textrm{d}y = \int e^{2y+1}\, \textrm{d}y = \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[ \begin{align*} \int (y^2+4)e^{2y+1}\, \textrm{d}y &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \left(y^2+4 \right)\left(\dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}\right)\left(2y \right)\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(y^2+4)e^{2y+1}}{2} - \int y\,e^{2y+1}\,\textrm{d}y. \end{align*} \]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int y\,e^{2y+1}\,\textrm{d}y.$ We take

\[\begin{align*}u=y\quad &\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y} = 1\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} = e^{2y+1}\quad & \Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} \,\textrm{d}y = \int e^{2y+1} \,\textrm{d}y = \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int y\,e^{2y+1}\,\textrm{d}y&= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \left(y \right)\left(\dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}\right) - \int \left( \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{2}\right)\left(1 \right)\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y\,e^{2y+1}}{2} -\dfrac{1}{2}\int e^{2y+1} \,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y\,e^{2y+1}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{4} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \[\begin{align*} \int (y^2+4)e^{2y+1} \,\textrm{d}y &= \dfrac{(y^2+4)e^{2y+1}}{2} - \int y\,e^{2y+1}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(y^2+4)e^{2y+1}}{2} - \left(\dfrac{y\,e^{2y+1}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{4} + D \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(y^2+4)e^{2y+1}}{2} - \dfrac{y\,e^{2y+1}}{2} + \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{4} - D \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{4}\left(2y^2 - 2y + 9\right)+ C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -{D}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: \[\begin{align*} \int_0^2 (y^2+4)e^{2y+1} \, \textrm{d} y &= \left[ \dfrac{e^{2y+1}}{4}\left(2y^2 - 2y + 9\right)\right]_0^2\\[5pt] &=\left( \dfrac{e^{2(2)+1}}{4}\left(2(2)^2 - 2(2) + 9\right) \right) - \left(\dfrac{e^{2(0)+1}}{4}\left(2(0)^2 - 2(0) + 9\right) \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{e^5}{4}(8-4+9) - \dfrac{e}{4}(0-0+9) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{13e^5}{4} - \dfrac{9e}{4} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{13e^5-9e}{4}} \end{align*}\]

example.title: Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*} u=3x^2+2 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 6x \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{3x} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int e^{3x} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}. \end{align*} \]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int (3x^2+2)e^{3x} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(3x^2+2\right)\left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}\right)\left(6x \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(3x^2+2)e^{3x}}{3} -\dfrac{6}{3}\int xe^{3x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(3x^2+2)e^{3x}}{3} -2\int xe^{3x}\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int xe^{3x}\,\textrm{d}x.$ We take

\[ \begin{align*} u=x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{3x} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int e^{3x} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int xe^{3x}\,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= x\left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{e^{3x}}{3}\right)(1)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{xe^{3x}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\int e^{3x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{xe^{3x}}{3} -\dfrac{e^{3x}}{9} + D\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{e^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have \[\begin{align*} \int (3x^2+2)e^{3x}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{(3x^2+2)e^{3x}}{3} -2\left( \dfrac{e^{3x}}{9}(3x-1)+D\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(3x^2+2)e^{3x}}{3} - \dfrac{2e^{3x}}{9}(3x-1) - 2D\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{3x}}{9}(3(3x^2 + 2) -2(3x -1)) - 2D\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{3x}}{9}(9x^2 - 6x + 8) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C =-2D .$

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \begin{align*} u=t^2 \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t} = 2t, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 3e^{2t+2} \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}\, \textrm{d}t = \int 3e^{2t+2}\, \textrm{d}t = \dfrac{3}{2}e^{2t+2}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} \int 3t^2e^{2t+2}\, \textrm{d}t &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t}\,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \left(t^2 \right)\left(\dfrac{3}{2}e^{2t+2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{3}{2}e^{2t+2}\right)\left(2t \right)\,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}t^2e^{2t+2} -3\int te^{2t+2}\,\textrm{d}t. \end{align*}

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {te^{2t+2}} \,\textrm{d}t.$ We take \begin{align*} u=t \quad &\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t} = 1, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = e^{2t+2} \quad &\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}\, \textrm{d}t = \int e^{2t+2} \,\textrm{d}t = \dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t+2}. \end{align*}

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \begin{align*} \int te^{2t+2} \,\textrm{d}t &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t}\,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \left(t \right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t+2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t+2}\right)\left(1 \right)\,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}te^{2t+2} -\dfrac{1}{2}\int e^{2t+2}\,\textrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}te^{2t+2} -\dfrac{1}{4}e^{2t+2} + D, \end{align*} where $D$ is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \begin{align*} \int 3t^2e^{2t+2}\, \textrm{d}t &= \dfrac{3}{2}t^2e^{2t+2} -3\int te^{2t+2}\,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}t^2e^{2t+2} - 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}te^{2t+2} -\dfrac{1}{4}e^{2t+2} + D \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}t^2e^{2t+2} -\dfrac{3}{2}te^{2t+2} +\dfrac{3}{4}e^{2t+2} + C, \end{align*} where $C=-3D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral: \begin{align*} \int_0^1 3t^2e^{2t+2} \,\textrm{d}t &=\left( \dfrac{3}{2}t^2e^{2t+2} -\dfrac{3}{2}te^{2t+2} +\dfrac{3}{4}e^{2t+2} \right) \, \Bigg|_0^1\\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(1^2)e^{2(1)+2}-\dfrac{3}{2}(1)e^{2(1)+2}+\dfrac{3}{4}e^{2(1)+2}\right)- \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(0^2)e^{2(0)+2}-\dfrac{3}{2}(0)e^{2(0)+2}+\dfrac{3}{4}e^{2(0)+2}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4}e^{4}-\dfrac{3}{4}e^{2}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3e^4-3e^2}{4}} \end{align*}

example.title: Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \begin{align*} u=z^2+1 \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z} = 2z, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z} = 4e^{2z} \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z}\, \textrm{d}z = 4\int e^{2z}\, \textrm{d}z = 2e^{2z}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} \int 4(z^2+1)e^{2z}\, \textrm{d}z &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= (z^2+1)\left(2e^{2z}\right) - \int (2e^{2z})\left(2z\right)\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= 2(z^2+1)e^{2z} - 4\int ze^{2z} \, \textrm{d}z . \end{align*}

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {ze^{2z}} \textrm{d}z.$ We take

\begin{align*}u=z\quad &\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z} =1\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z} = e^{2z}\quad & \Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z} \,\textrm{d}z =\int e^{2z} \,\textrm{d}z = \dfrac{e^{2z}}{2}. \end{align*}

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \begin{align*} \int ze^{2z}\, \textrm{d}z &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= \left(z \right)\left(\dfrac{e^{2z}}{2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{e^{2z}}{2}\right)\left(1\right)\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ze^{2z}}{2} -\dfrac{1}{2}\int e^{2z} \,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{ze^{2z}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2z}}{4} + D, \end{align*} where $D$ is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \begin{align*} \int 4(z^2+1)e^{2z} \, \textrm{d} z&= 2(z^2+1)e^{2z} - 4\int ze^{2z} \, \textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= 2(z^2+1)e^{2z} - 4\left(\dfrac{ze^{2z}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2z}}{4} + D\right) \\[5pt] &= 2(z^2+1)e^{2z} - 2ze^{2z} + e^{2z} + C, \end{align*} where $C = -{4D}.$

Finally, then, we can work out the definite integral: \begin{align*} \int_0^1 4(z^2+1)e^{2z} \, \textrm{d} z &= \left(2(z^2+1)e^{2z} - 2ze^{2z} + e^{2z} \right)\bigg|_0^1\\[5pt] &=\left( 2(1^2+1)\left(e\right)^{2} - {2(1)^2 e^{2}}+{e^{2}} \right) - \left( 2\left(0+1\right)e^{0} - {2\cdot 0 \cdot e^0}+{e^0} \right)\\[5pt] &= 3e^2-3\end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \begin{align*} u=y^2+3 \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y} = 2y, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} = e^{2y-1} \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\, \textrm{d}y = \int e^{2y-1}\, \textrm{d}y = \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[ \begin{align*} \int (y^2+3)e^{2y-1}\, \textrm{d}y &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \left(y^2+3 \right)\left(\dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}\right)\left(2y \right)\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(y^2+3)e^{2y-1}}{2} - \int y\,e^{2y-1}\,\textrm{d}y. \end{align*} \]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int y\,e^{2y-1}\,\textrm{d}y.$ We take

\[\begin{align*}u=y\quad &\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y} = 1\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} = e^{2y-1}\quad & \Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y} \,\textrm{d}y = \int e^{2y-1} \,\textrm{d}y = \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int y\,e^{2y-1}\,\textrm{d}y&= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \left(y \right)\left(\dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}\right) - \int \left( \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{2}\right)\left(1 \right)\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y\,e^{2y-1}}{2} -\dfrac{1}{2}\int e^{2y-1} \,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y\,e^{2y-1}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{4} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \[\begin{align*} \int (y^2+3)e^{2y-1} \,\textrm{d}y &= \dfrac{(y^2+3)e^{2y-1}}{2} - \int y\,e^{2y-1}\,\textrm{d}y\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(y^2+3)e^{2y-1}}{2} - \left(\dfrac{y\,e^{2y-1}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{4} + D \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(y^2+3)e^{2y-1}}{2} - \dfrac{y\,e^{2y-1}}{2} + \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{4} - D \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{4}\left(2y^2 - 2y + 7\right)+ C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -{D}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: \[\begin{align*} \int_1^2 (y^2+3)e^{2y-1} \, \textrm{d} y &= \left[ \dfrac{e^{2y-1}}{4}\left(2y^2 - 2y + 7\right)\right]_1^2\\[5pt] &=\left( \dfrac{e^{2(2)-1}}{4}\left(2(2)^2 - 2(2) + 7\right) \right) - \left(\dfrac{e^{2(1)-1}}{4}\left(2(1)^2 - 2(1) + 7\right) \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{e^3}{4}(8-4+7) - \dfrac{e}{4}(2-2+7) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{11e^3}{4} - \dfrac{7e}{4} \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{11e^3-7e}{4}} \end{align*}\]

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define \begin{align*} u=x^2 \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(2x) \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int \cos(2x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

\[\begin{align*} \int x^2\cos(2x) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x^2\right)\left(\dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}\right)\left(2x \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2\sin(2x)}{2} - \int x\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

example.title: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*} u=x^2+3x \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x+3 \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(x) \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int \sin(x) \,\textrm{d}x = -\cos(x). \end{align*} \]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[ \begin{align*} \int (x^2+3x)\sin(x)\, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x^2 +3x\right)(-\cos(x)) - \int (-\cos(x))\left(2x+3 \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -(x^2+3x)\cos(x) +2\int x\cos(x)\textrm{d}x +3\int \cos(x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -(x^2+3x)\cos(x) +2\int x\cos(x)\textrm{d}x + 3\sin(x). \end{align*} \]

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle{\int x\cos(x)\,\textrm{d}x}.$ We take \[ \begin{align*} u=x \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(x) \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \textrm{d}x = \int \cos(x)\, \textrm{d}x = \sin(x). \end{align*} \]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[ \begin{align*} \int x\cos(x) \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x \right)(\sin(x)) - \int (\sin(x))\left(1 \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= x\sin(x) -\int \sin(x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= x\sin(x) + \cos(x) + D, \end{align*} \] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have \[ \begin{align*} \int (x^2+3x)\sin(x)\, \textrm{d}x &= -(x^2+3x)\cos(x) +2(x\sin(x) + \cos(x) +D)+3\sin(x) \\[5pt] &= -(x^2+3x)\cos(x) + 2x\sin(x) + 2\cos(x) + C + 3\sin(x)\\[5pt] &= (-x^2-3x+2)\cos(x) + (2x+3)\sin(x) + C, \end{align*} \] where $C = 2D.$

example.title: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \[\begin{align*} u=x^2+1 \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos x \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int \cos x\, \textrm{d}x = {\sin x}. \end{align*}\]

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int (x^2+1)\cos x\, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x^2+1\right)(\sin x) - \int (\sin x)\left(2x \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (x^2+1)\sin x - 2\int x\sin x \,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x\sin x\,\textrm{d}x.$ We take \[\begin{align*} u=x &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} =\sin x&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \sin x \,\textrm{d}x = -\cos x\,. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \begin{align} \int x\sin x\,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= x(-\cos x) - \int (-\cos x)(1)\mathrm dx\\[5pt] &= -x \cos x + \int \cos x\,\mathrm dx\\[5pt] &= -x \cos x + \sin x + D, \end{align} where $D$ is an integral constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \begin{align} \int (x^2+1)\cos x\, \textrm{d}x& = (x^2+1)\sin x -2\int x\sin x \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= (x^2+1)\sin x - 2(-x \cos x + \sin x + D)\\[5pt] &=(x^2+1)\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x + C\\ \end{align}

where $C = -2D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: \begin{align} \int_0^{\pi} (x^2+1)\cos x\, \textrm{d}x &= \left[ (x^2+1)\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x\right]_0^\pi \\[5pt] &= (\pi^2+1)\sin\pi + 2\pi\cos\pi - 2\sin\pi- ((0^2+1)\sin 0 + 2\cdot 0 \cdot \cos 0 - 2\sin 0)\\[5pt] &= (\pi^2+1)\cdot 0 + 2\pi(-1) - 2\cdot 0 - 0\\[5pt] &=-2\pi \end{align}

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*} u=x^2+2x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x+2 \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(x) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x = \int \cos(x)\, \textrm{d}x = \sin(x). \end{align*} \]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int (x^2+2x)\cos(x) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x^2 +2x\right)(\sin(x)) - \int (\sin(x))\left(2x+2 \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (x^2+2x)\sin(x) -2\int x\sin(x)\textrm{d}x - 2\int \sin(x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (x^2+2x)\sin(x) -2\int x\sin(x)\textrm{d}x + 2\cos(x). \end{align*}\]

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x\sin(x)\,\textrm{d}x.$ We take

\[ \begin{align*} u=x\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(x) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int \sin(x) \,\textrm{d}x = -\cos(x). \end{align*} \]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int x\sin(x) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(x \right)(-\cos(x)) - \int (-\cos(x))\left(1 \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -x\cos(x) +\int \cos(x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -x\cos(x) + \sin(x) + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have \[\begin{align*} \int (x^2+2x)\cos(x) \,\textrm{d}x &= (x^2+2x)\sin(x) -2(-x\cos(x) + \sin(x) +D)+2\cos(x) \\[5pt] &= (x^2+2x)\sin(x) + 2x\cos(x) - 2\sin(x) + C + 2\cos(x)\\[5pt] &= (x^2+2x-2)\sin(x) + 2(x+1)\cos(x) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -2D.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*} u=(\log_2 x)^2 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\log_2x}{x\ln 2} \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 1 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int\,\textrm{d}x = x. \end{align*}\]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int (\log_2 x)^2\, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\ &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\ &= \left(\log_2 x\right)^2(x) - \int (x)\left(\dfrac{2\log_2 x}{x\ln 2} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\ &= x\left(\log_2 x\right)^2 - \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\int {\log_2 x} \,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle \int \log_2 (x)\,\textrm{d}x.$ We take \[ \begin{align*} u=\log_2 x\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{x\ln 2} \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 1\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int \,\textrm{d}x = {x}. \end{align*} \]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int \log_2 x\, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\ &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\ &= \left(\log_2 x \right)(x) - \int (x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x\ln 2} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\ &= x\log_2 x -\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\int\, \textrm{d}x\\ &=x\log_2 x -\dfrac{x}{\ln 2} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have \[\begin{align*} \int (\log_2 x)^2 \,\textrm{d}x &= x\left(\log_2 x\right)^2 - \dfrac{2}{\ln 2}\left (x\log_2 x -\dfrac{x}{\ln 2} + D\right)\\[5pt] &= x\left(\log_2 x\right)^2 - \dfrac{2x\log_2 x}{\ln 2}+\dfrac{2x}{\ln^2 2} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{x\ln^2x }{\ln^2 2} - \dfrac{2x\ln x}{\ln^2 2}+\dfrac{2x}{\ln^2 2} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{x}{\ln^2 2}\left(\ln^2x - 2\ln x+2\right) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C = - \dfrac{2D}{\ln 2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula $\log_2{x}=\dfrac{\ln{x}}{\ln{2}}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: \[\begin{align*} \int_1^{e} (\log_ 2 x)^2 \, \textrm{d}x &= \left[ \dfrac{x}{\ln^2 2}\left(\ln^2x - 2\ln x+2\right) \right]_1^e\\[1ex] &= \dfrac{e}{\ln^2 2}\left(\ln^2e - 2\ln e+2\right)- \dfrac{1}{\ln^2 2}\left(\ln^2 1 - 2\ln 1+2\right)\\[1ex] &= \dfrac{e}{\ln^2 2}- \dfrac{2}{\ln^2 2}\\[1ex] &= \dfrac{e - 2}{\ln^2 2}.\end{align*}\]

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \[\begin{align*} u=(\ln(x+1))^2 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\ln(x+1)}{x+1}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 27(x+1)^2 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int 27(x+1)^2\,\textrm{d}x = 9(x+1)^3. \end{align*}\]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int 27(x+1)^2(\ln(x+1))^2 \, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2\left(9(x+1)^3\right) - \int \left(9(x+1)^3\right)\left(\dfrac{2\ln(x+1)}{x+1} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 9(x+1)^3\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 -18\int {(x+1)^2\ln(x+1)}\, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {(x+1)^2\ln(x+1)} \, \textrm{d}x.$ We take \[\begin{align*} u=\ln(x+1) &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} =(x+1)^2&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int (x+1)^2 \, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{(x+1)^3}{3}\,. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int (x+1)^2\ln(x+1) \, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln(x+1)\left( \dfrac{(x+1)^3}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{(x+1)^3}{3} \right)\left(\dfrac{1}{x+1} \right) \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(x+1)^3\ln(x+1)}{3}-\dfrac{1}{3}\int (x+1)^2 \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(x+1)^3\ln(x+1)}{3} -\dfrac{(x+1)^3}{9} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \[\begin{align*} \int 27(x+1)^2(\ln(x+1))^2 \, \textrm{d}x & = 9(x+1)^3\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 -18\int {(x+1)^2\ln(x+1)} \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 9(x+1)^3\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 -18\left(\dfrac{(x+1)^3\ln(x+1)}{3} -\dfrac{(x+1)^3}{9} + D\right)\\[5pt] &= 9(x+1)^3\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 - 6(x+1)^3\ln(x+1)+2(x+1)^3 - 18D\\[5pt] &= (x+1)^3\left(9\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 - 6\ln(x+1)+2 \right) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -18D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral: \begin{align*} \int_0^{e-1} 27(x+1)^2(\ln(x+1))^2 \textrm{d}x &=\left[ (x+1)^3\left(9\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^2 - 6\ln(x+1)+2 \right) \right]_0^{e-1}\\[5pt] &=\left[ e^3\left(9\left(\ln e\right)^2 - 6\ln e+2 \right) \right] - \left[1^3\left(9\left(\ln 1\right)^2 - 6\ln 1+2 \right) \right]\\[5pt] &=\left[e^3\left(9 - 6 + 2 \right)\right] - 2 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 5e^3 - 2} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*}u=(\log_3 x)^2 \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\log_3 x}{x\ln 3}\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 4x \quad & \Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int 4x\,\textrm{d}x = 2x^2. \end{align*} \]

This gives \[ \begin{align*} \int 4x(\log_3 x)^2\, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(\log_3 x \right)^2( 2x^2) - \int (2x^2)\left(\dfrac{2\log_3 x}{x\ln 3} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 2x^2 (\log_3 x)^2 - \dfrac{4}{\ln 3}\int {x\log_3(x)} \,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*} \]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {x\log_3(x)} \textrm{d}x.$ We take

\[\begin{align*}u=\log_3(x)\quad &\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{x\ln 3}\\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = x \quad & \Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int x \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^2}{2}. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int x\log_3 x\, \textrm{d}x&= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(\log_ 3 x \right)\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{x\ln 3} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2\log_3 x}{2} -\dfrac{1}{2\ln 3}\int x \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{x^2\log_3 x}{2} - \dfrac{x^2}{4\ln 3} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \[\begin{align*} \int 4x(\log_3 x)^2 \,\textrm{d}x &= 2x^2 (\log_3 x)^2 - \dfrac{4}{\ln 3}\left (\dfrac{x^2\log_3 x}{2} - \dfrac{x^2}{4\ln 3} + D\right)\\[5pt] &=2x^2 (\log_3 x)^2 - \dfrac{2x^2\log_3 x}{\ln 3} + \dfrac{x^2}{\ln^2 3} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2x^2 \ln^2 x}{\ln^2 3} - \dfrac{2x^2\ln x}{\ln^2 3} + \dfrac{x^2}{\ln^2 3} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{x^2}{\ln^2 3}\left( 2\ln^2 x - 2\ln x + 1\right) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -\dfrac{4D}{\ln 3}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula $\log_3{x}=\dfrac{\ln{x}}{\ln{3}}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: \[\begin{align*} \int_1^{e} 4x(\log_3 x)^2 \, \textrm{d}x &= \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{\ln^2 3}\left( 2\ln^2 x - 2\ln x + 1\right)\right]_1^e\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^2}{\ln^2 3}\left( 2\ln^2 e - 2\ln e + 1\right)- \dfrac{1^2}{\ln^2 3}\left( 2\ln^2 1 - 2\ln 1 + 1\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^2}{\ln^2 3}\left( 2 - 2 + 1\right)- \dfrac{1}{\ln^2 3}\left( 0 - 0 + 1\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^2-1}{\ln^2 3}.\end{align*}\]

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define \[\begin{align*} u=(\ln(3x))^2 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\ln(3x)}{x}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int 3\,\textrm{d}x = 3x. \end{align*}\]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int 3(\ln(3x))^2 \, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (\ln(3x))^2(3x) - \int (3x)\left(\dfrac{2\ln(3x)}{x} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 3x(\ln(3x))^2 - \int 6\ln(3x)\, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {6\ln(3x)} \, \textrm{d}x.$ We take \[\begin{align*} u=\ln(3x) &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{x}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 6 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int 6 \, \textrm{d}x = 6x. \end{align*}\]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int 6\ln(3x) \, \textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln(3x)(6x) - \int (6x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x} \right) \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 6x\ln(3x) - \int 6 \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 6x\ln(3x) - 6x + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is \[\begin{align*} \int 3(\ln(3x))^2 \, \textrm{d}x & = 3x(\ln(3x))^2 - \int 6\ln(3x) \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 3x(\ln(3x))^2 - (6x\ln(3x) - 6x + D)\\[5pt] &= 3x(\ln(3x))^2 - 6x\ln(3x) + 6x - D\\[5pt] &= 3x\left((\ln(3x))^2 - 2\ln(3x) + 2 \right) + C, \end{align*}\] where $C = -D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral: \begin{align*} \int_{1/3}^{e/3} 3(\ln(3x))^2 \textrm{d}x &=\left[ 3x\left((\ln(3x))^2 - 2\ln(3x) + 2 \right) \right]_{1/3}^{e/3}\\[5pt] &=\left[ 3\left(\dfrac{e}{3}\right)\left(\left(\ln\left(3\cdot\dfrac{e}{3}\right)\right)^2 - 2\ln\left(3\cdot\dfrac{e}{3}\right) + 2 \right) \right] - \left[3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\left(\left(\ln\left(3\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right)^2 - 2\ln\left(3\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + 2 \right) \right]\\[5pt] &=\left[e\left((\ln e)^2 - 2\ln e + 2 \right)\right] - \left[ 1\left((\ln 1)^2 - 2\ln 1 + 2 \right) \right] \\[5pt] &=\left[e\left(1 - 2 + 2 \right)\right] - \left[ 1(0 - 0 + 2) \right] \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ e - 2} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define \[ \begin{align*} u=\left(\ln x^2\right)^2\quad &\Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2 \ln x^2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^2} \cdot 2x = \dfrac{4\ln x^2}{x} \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = 4x^2 \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} \,\textrm{d}x = \int 4x^2\,\,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{4x^3}{3}. \end{align*} \]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \[\begin{align*} \int 4x^2\left(\ln x^2\right)^2 \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(\ln x^2\right)^2\left(\dfrac{4x^3}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{4x^3}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{4\ln x^2}{x} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4x^3\left(\ln x^2\right)^2}{3} - \dfrac{16}{3}\int {x^2\ln(x^2)} \,\textrm{d}x. \end{align*}\]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {x^2\ln(x^2)} \textrm{d}x.$ We take \[ \begin{align*} u=\ln(x^2) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{x} \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = x^2\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\, \textrm{d}x = \int x^2 \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^3}{3}. \end{align*} \]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives \[\begin{align*} \int x^2\ln(x^2) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left(\ln(x^2) \right)\left( \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{x^3}{3} \right)\left(\dfrac{2}{x} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3\ln(x^2)}{3}-\dfrac{2}{3}\int x^2\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3\ln(x^2)}{3} -\dfrac{2x^3}{9} + D, \end{align*}\] where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have \[\begin{align*} \int 4x^2\left(\ln x^2\right)^2\,\textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{4x^3\left(\ln x^2\right)^2}{3} -\dfrac{16}{3}\left( \dfrac{x^3\ln(x^2)}{3} -\dfrac{2x^3}{9} + D\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4x^3\left(\ln x^2\right)^2}{3} - \dfrac{16x^3\ln(x^2)}{9} +\dfrac{32x^3}{27} -\dfrac{16D}{3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4x^3}{27}\left(9\left(\ln{x^2}\right)^2 - 12\ln{x^2} + 8 \right) + C, \end{align*}\] Where, $C= -\dfrac{16D}{3}.$
